title: Liber Apologeticus
author: Paulus Orosius
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0215c.stoa002.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: ad haec Iohannes episcopus ut Pelagius coram intromitteretur expetiit. cui et propter paternitatis ipsius reuerentiam et propter actionis utilitatem, dum praesentem ab episcopo rectius crederetis confutandum, intromittendi coniuentia praestita est.
passages.english: At this Bishop John asked that Pelagius be brought in before [us]. Out of reverence for [John's] fatherly standing, and for the benefit of the proceedings, since you believed it more proper that he be refuted by the bishop while present, consent was given to bring him in.
passages.notes: The shift to the second person plural (crederetis, 'you believed') is in the Latin. Orosius may be addressing his fellow participants, or the text may be corrupt. 'paternitatis ipsius' is taken as referring to Bishop John.

passages.original: Intromissum Pelagium unanimiter omnes interrogastis, an haec, quibus Augustinus episcopus respondisset, se docuisse cognosceret. ilico ille respondit: cet quis est mihi Augustinus ?\' cumque uniuersi acclamarent, blasphemantem in episcopum, ex cuius ore Dominus uniuersae Africae unitatis indulserit sanitatem, non solum a conuentu illo uerum ab omni ecclesia pellendum, episcopus Iohannes ilico eum, hominem uidelicet laicum in consessu presbyterorum, reum haereseos manifestae in medio catholicorum sedere praecepit et deinde ait:
passages.english: When Pelagius had been brought in, you all with one voice asked him whether he acknowledged that he had taught these things to which Bishop Augustine had replied. At once he answered: "And who is Augustine to me?" And when everyone cried out that one who blasphemed against the bishop, through whose mouth the Lord had granted to all Africa the restored health of unity, should be driven out not only from that assembly but from the whole Church, Bishop John at once ordered him, a layman in fact, to sit in the session of the presbyters, a man guilty of manifest heresy seated in the midst of catholics, and then said:
passages.notes: "cet" is evidently a scanning error for "et"; the stray "\'" after the question mark is a mark of the scan. The Latin is awkward around "hominem uidelicet laicum in consessu presbyterorum, reum haereseos manifestae in medio catholicorum sedere". These phrases are probably Orosius's indignant apposition: a layman seated among presbyters, a manifest heretic among catholics. The translation keeps them as appositions.

passages.original: multisque aliis actitatis Iohannes episcopus nouissimam sententiam protulit, confirmans tandem postulationem intentionemque nostram, ut ad beatum Innocentium, papam Romanum, fratres et epistulae mitterentur, uniuersis quod ille decerneret secuturis, sed ut haereticus Pelagius imposito sibi eatenus silentio conticesceret et ut nostri ab insultatione conuicti Iohannis confessique cessarent. uniuersi in hanc sententiam consensimus; gratiarum actione celebrata, pace facta et consummata ad pacis testimonium oratione discessimus.
passages.english: After many other matters had been dealt with, Bishop John delivered his final judgement. In the end he confirmed our request and purpose: that brothers and letters should be sent to the blessed Innocent, pope of Rome, and that all would follow whatever he decided. Meanwhile the heretic Pelagius was to keep silent, a silence being imposed on him until then, and our people were to cease from insulting John, since he had been refuted and had confessed. We all agreed to this judgement. Thanks were given, peace was made, and when a prayer had been completed as a witness to the peace, we departed.
passages.notes: 'ut nostri ab insultatione conuicti Iohannis confessique cessarent' is difficult. It is taken here as 'our people should stop insulting John, [now] refuted and having confessed.' 'conuicti … confessique' may instead refer to Pelagius, giving the sense 'insulting [Pelagius] as refuted and self-confessed', and 'Iohannis' would then be displaced or corrupt. The reading is uncertain.
